question: A metrics service ingests 500,000 new data points per second, each with a new key, and rarely reads old points. Which storage engine family fits best?
options: A B-tree engine, because its pages are updated in place
An LSM tree engine, because writes become sequential WAL appends and batched SSTable flushes
Either: write rates do not depend on the storage engine
A B-tree engine with a smaller page size, so splits never happen
explanation: An LSM tree buffers writes in the MemTable and writes them to disk sequentially in large sorted batches. A B-tree turns random new keys into random page writes and page splits.

question: An LSM store holds `user:7` in an old SSTable. The application deletes `user:7`, and the developer implements the delete by removing the key from the MemTable. What does the next `get('user:7')` return?
options: Nothing, because the MemTable is always checked first
An error, because the key is in an immutable file
The old value from the SSTable, because nothing newer shadows it; the delete needed a tombstone
Nothing, because compaction runs on every read
explanation: SSTables are immutable and reads fall through to older files when the MemTable has no entry. Only a tombstone, a newer entry marking the delete, stops the read before the old value.

question: Reads of keys that do not exist are slow on an LSM store with 40 SSTables. Which mechanism makes such reads cheap?
options: A Bloom filter per SSTable, which answers "definitely not here" so the file is skipped without disk access
A larger WAL, so every key is found there first
Disabling compaction, so fewer files are rewritten
Updating SSTables in place, so each key lives in one file
explanation: A missing key would otherwise be searched in every SSTable. Bloom filters have no false negatives, so a "no" safely skips the file; compaction also lowers the number of files to check.

question: A team switches an LSM store from size-tiered to leveled compaction. What trade-off should they expect?
options: No trade-off: leveled compaction is better in every dimension
Higher read amplification and more disk space used
Tombstones are no longer needed for deletes
Lower read and space amplification, paid for with higher write amplification because data is rewritten more often
explanation: Leveled compaction keeps non-overlapping key ranges in every level below level 0, so a read touches at most one file in each of them and old versions disappear quickly, but each byte is rewritten as it moves down the levels.

question: Why does an LSM tree append each write to the write-ahead log before inserting it into the MemTable?
options: The WAL keeps keys sorted for range scans
The MemTable lives in memory, so after a crash the WAL is replayed to rebuild the writes that were not flushed yet
The WAL replaces the SSTables once it is large enough
Bloom filters are built from the WAL
explanation: Memory is lost on a crash. A sequential append to the WAL makes the write durable cheaply; once the MemTable is flushed to an SSTable, that part of the log can be discarded.

question: An order database runs short transactions that update existing rows, plus range queries by date for reports. Writes are moderate. Which engine is the sensible default?
options: A B-tree engine such as InnoDB or PostgreSQL, which favors point reads, range scans and in-place updates
An LSM engine, because every workload is write-heavy eventually
An append-only log with no index
An LSM engine with compaction disabled to avoid write amplification
explanation: B-trees give low read amplification and efficient range scans over sorted pages. Their write cost only dominates when the write rate is very high, which this workload does not have.
